title: One Prompt Can Fabricate a Disaster: Cybersecurity Bureau of the Ministry of Public Security Releases 10 Typical Cases of AI-Generated Rumors

content_html:
Creating rumors with AI is no longer an isolated phenomenon; it has become a categorized offense publicly reported in batches. On November 24, the cybersecurity departments of public security authorities released 10 typical cases from 2026 involving the use of AI tools to fabricate and spread online rumors: in 3 cases, the individuals involved were placed under criminal coercive measures in accordance with law, and in 7 cases, administrative penalties were imposed.

Three Criminal Cases: Disasters and Police Uniforms

The three cases in which criminal coercive measures were taken centered on two types of content most likely to trigger panic. A person surnamed Ma used AI to generate a video titled “Sudden Collapse of the Zhangjiajie Grand Canyon Glass Bridge”—in the footage, the glass bridge breaks and crowds flee in all directions, with the caption “If you have nothing to do, don’t go out to play,” causing public panic; a person surnamed Wu fabricated “Guangzhou Huadu Night Market Flooded by Heavy Rain,” in which the water is nearly as high as the power lines, even though there was no disaster in the area; and a person surnamed Han put on the official uniform of the People’s Police and, together with police insignia and a police car, generated false images and videos to mislead internet users.

Seven Administrative Cases: From Exam Scores to Toxic Rice

The remaining seven cases resulted only in administrative penalties, but their scenarios covered almost every area of life: a person surnamed Sun fabricated a “Lianyungang Seizure of a 4.6 Billion Yuan Rare Earth Smuggling Case”; a person surnamed Wang, disgruntled as a fan, used AI to forge a social media post by an artist, impersonating the artist’s voice to complain that a performance had been halted; a person surnamed Zhou fabricated “Estimated Gaokao Score of 715 but Actual Score 299; Answer Sheet Switched”; a person surnamed Shu generated a video of an “Artificial Toxic Rice Production Line in Hubei”; a person surnamed Cao fabricated false news that norovirus had caused “multiple schools to suspend classes”; two people surnamed Wang and Zhang, riding the hot topic of a “school uniform incident,” used AI to fabricate a video claiming that another school’s uniforms contained plastic; and a person surnamed Xing, in order to sell products via livestreaming, started a livestream by unauthorized use of a public figure’s image.

Looking across the ten cases, the motives were mostly to attract followers and drive traffic, with some for venting emotions or profiting from product sales—the common point is that AI has reduced the cost of spreading rumors to a single prompt, while the legal consequences have not been lowered accordingly.
